legal_framework.crown_copyright_rule: Section 163 CDPA 1988: Crown Copyright in published photographic and artistic works expires 50 years after the end of the calendar year of publication. All UK official government and military works published prior to 1976 reside in the worldwide Public Domain.
legal_framework.us_statute: 17 U.S. Code § 105: Works prepared by officers or employees of the United States Federal Government as part of official duties reside in the Public Domain upon creation.
legal_framework.layer2_illustrative_policy: 100% of Layer 2 decorative narrative plates, cover artworks, visual story sheets, and individual portraits use strictly Public Domain works, statutory Freedom of Panorama (CDPA s.62 / § 59 UrhG), or open commercial-permitted licences (CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA 3.0/4.0, Open Government Licence v3.0). Zero reliance on non-commercial CDPA s.32.
legal_framework.layer3_criticism_quotation_rule: Section 30(1) & Section 30(1ZA) CDPA 1988: In-copyright primary historical sources and historiographical extracts in Layer 3 disciplinary enquiries are reproduced exclusively for genuine historical criticism, provenance evaluation, and scholarly quotation, accompanied by full attribution of creator, date, and holding repository.
legal_framework.open_access_standards: Creative Commons Attribution (CC BY 4.0 / CC BY-SA 3.0 / CC BY-SA 4.0) and Open Government Licence v3.0 (OGL).

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.0: Broken Promises & Imperial Borders: Why Was Conflict in the Middle East Inevitable?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Mutiny of German Sailors at Kiel
sources.creator: Imperial Press / Naval Photographer
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Kiel Sailors' Revolt (November 1918): Armed sailors seized battleships and formed revolutionary workers' and soldiers' councils, setting off an unstoppable collapse of imperial military authority.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the mutiny of sailors at Kiel trigger an unstoppable revolution across Germany when frontline armies had not yet been formally breached?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Opening Session of the National Assembly in Weimar
sources.creator: German Press Photojournalist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Weimar National Assembly (February 1919): Democratic delegates convened in Weimar to escape civil unrest in Berlin, drafting Europe's most progressive democratic constitution.
sources.hinge_question: Why did holding the National Assembly in the quiet cultural town of Weimar symbolize both democratic idealism and the physical vulnerability of the new republic?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Proclamation of the Republic by Philipp Scheidemann
sources.creator: German Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: SPD leader Philipp Scheidemann proclaiming the German Republic from a window of the Reichstag building in Berlin to pre-empt a communist declaration.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Scheidemann rush to proclaim a parliamentary republic from the Reichstag window without consulting party leader Friedrich Ebert?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Armed Workers and Soldiers Manning Barricades in Berlin
sources.creator: Berlin Revolutionary Press Agency
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Armed revolutionary fighters and deserting soldiers manning a street barricade constructed from giant newsprint rolls in the Berlin newspaper quarter during the revolutionary unrest of 1918–1919.
sources.hinge_question: How does Source B illustrate why Friedrich Ebert felt compelled to make a secret alliance with the imperial military officer corps in the Ebert-Groener Pact?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Weimar Constitution Official Title Page (Reichsgesetzblatt)
sources.creator: Reichsministerium des Innern / Hugo Preuß
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official German State Charter / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: Official title page of the Weimar Constitution (Reichsgesetzblatt 1919), establishing a democratic republic with universal suffrage and emergency presidential decrees under Article 48.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the inclusion of Article 48 in the Weimar Constitution ultimately prove more dangerous to democracy than the proportional representation voting system?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Proclamation of Abdication of Wilhelm II by Prince Max von Baden
sources.creator: Imperial Chancellery, Berlin
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official Imperial Decree / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: Imperial government decree issued by Prince Max von Baden announcing that Kaiser Wilhelm II and the Crown Prince had renounced the throne, transferring power to Friedrich Ebert.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Prince Max von Baden announce the Kaiser's abdication before Wilhelm II had personally signed an official instrument of renunciation?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.1: The Origins of the Republic, 1918–1919
sources.artifact_title: Address to the Weimar National Assembly by Reich President Friedrich Ebert
sources.creator: Friedrich Ebert (Reich President of the Weimar Republic)
sources.repository: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv), Berlin / Reichstag Protocols
sources.accession_id: Verhandlungen der verfassunggebenden Deutschen Nationalversammlung, Vol. 326
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official Government Speech Delivered 1919 — CDPA 1988 / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: Reich President Friedrich Ebert delivering the keynote opening address to the newly elected Weimar National Assembly on 6 February 1919.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Friedrich Ebert emphasise both lawful democratic order at home and resistance to Allied vengeance abroad in his opening address?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Territorial Losses under the Treaty of Versailles (1919)
sources.creator: Allied Peace Commission / German Cartographic Institute
sources.repository: National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) / Imperial War Museum
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Cartography)
sources.caption: Versailles Territorial Losses (1919): Germany surrendered 13% of its European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine and the Polish Corridor, separating East Prussia from the German mainland.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the geographic division of East Prussia by the Polish Corridor particularly humiliating to the German military establishment?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Children Playing with Banknote Bricks during Hyperinflation
sources.creator: German Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: The Hyperinflation Catastrophe (1923): Money lost its value so rapidly that millions of marks were bundled into bricks for children's games, permanently wiping out middle-class life savings.
sources.hinge_question: How did hyperinflation permanently destroy the Weimar middle class's faith in democratic governance, even after the currency was stabilized?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: The "Stab in the Back" (Dolchstoßlegende) Nationalist Postcard
sources.creator: Austrian Nationalist Publisher
sources.repository: Austrian National Library (ÖNB) / Imperial War Museum
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Published Propaganda)
sources.caption: Austrian and German right-wing postcard depicting the "Stab in the Back" (Dolchstoßlegende), claiming German frontline soldiers were betrayed from behind by socialist and Jewish home-front politicians.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the "Stab in the Back" myth so politically toxic for the long-term legitimacy of the Weimar democracy?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Marinebrigade Ehrhardt Freikorps during the Kapp Putsch
sources.creator: Berlin Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Mutinous soldiers of the Ehrhardt Naval Brigade wearing swastika-painted steel helmets occupying the government district in Berlin during the right-wing Kapp Putsch.
sources.hinge_question: Why did General von Seeckt declare that "Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr" when the Weimar government ordered the military to crush the Kapp Putsch?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: A One-Billion-Mark Overprinted Banknote (Eine Milliarde Mark) Issued by the Reichsbank during Peak Hyperinflation
sources.creator: Reichsbank Directorate, Berlin
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official German State Banknote / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: Official 1,000-Mark banknote overprinted in bold red gothic lettering with "Eine Milliarde Mark" (1,000,000,000 Mark / One Billion Mark) by the Reichsbank in Berlin during the peak hyperinflation crisis of late 1923, showing both obverse and reverse.
sources.hinge_question: Why did hyperinflation inflict far greater psychological trauma on the German middle class than on industrial tycoons who owned physical assets?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Eyewitness Account of the 1923 Hyperinflation by Erna von Pustau
sources.creator: Erna von Pustau (Hamburg Citizen and Eyewitness)
sources.repository: Hamburg State Archives / Contemporary Published Account
sources.accession_id: Erna von Pustau & Pearl S. Buck, The Way to Poverty (1923)
sources.rights_status: Educational Quotation / Public Domain (Historical Memoir Extract 1923 — Section 30 CDPA 1988)
sources.caption: Eyewitness diary account written by Erna von Pustau, recording the daily panic and social humiliation of hyperinflation in Hamburg in late 1923.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the 1923 hyperinflation destroy middle-class trust in parliamentary democracy far more deeply than the military defeat of 1918?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Revolutionary Soldiers at the Brandenburg Gate (Spartacist Uprising)
sources.creator: German Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Armed revolutionary troops occupying positions around the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin during the communist Spartacist Uprising led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the brutal suppression of the Spartacist Uprising create a permanent, irreconcilable hatred between the SPD and the Communist Party (KPD)?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The 1-Rentenmark Banknote Halting Hyperinflation
sources.creator: Deutsche Rentenbank, Berlin
sources.accession_id: Deutsche Rentenbank Berlin Serie A / 1 Rentenmark
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official German State Banknote / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: The Rentenmark Miracle (November 1923): Backed by agricultural mortgages and industrial assets, Gustav Stresemann's new currency abruptly restored public confidence and halted hyperinflation.
sources.hinge_question: Why was a psychological anchor—backing currency with industrial real estate rather than scarce gold—sufficient to restore public faith in the German currency?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Gustav Stresemann Addressing the League of Nations in Geneva
sources.creator: Photopress / Keystone Geneva
sources.rights_status: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 3.0 Germany (CC BY-SA 3.0 DE — Bundesarchiv)
sources.caption: Germany Enters the League of Nations (September 1926): Foreign Minister Stresemann delivered Germany's maiden address in Geneva, securing a permanent seat on the League Council as an equal great power.
sources.hinge_question: How did Germany's permanent Council seat in the League of Nations undermine right-wing claims that Weimar politicians were merely passive puppets of the victorious Allies?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Gustav Stresemann and European Foreign Ministers at Locarno
sources.creator: Swiss Press Agency / Keystone Press
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1925 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: German Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann with French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand and British Foreign Secretary Austen Chamberlain at Locarno, guaranteeing Germany's western borders.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Stresemann agree to guarantee Germany's western borders with France and Belgium while refusing to give similar guarantees for its eastern borders with Poland and Czechoslovakia?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: $1,000 Gold Bond Certificate for the Dawes Loan
sources.creator: German External Loan 1924 / J.P. Morgan & Co.
sources.repository: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Historical Archives
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Published Financial Security)
sources.caption: Official 7% Gold Bond certificate for $1,000 issued by the German government under the Dawes Plan, floated by J.P. Morgan & Co. in New York to finance German economic recovery.
sources.hinge_question: How did the Dawes Plan create a dangerous economic cycle where Germany relied entirely on American loans to pay British and French reparations?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The Signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact in Paris
sources.creator: French Foreign Ministry / Library of Congress
sources.repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, Washington D.C.
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Work of the US Federal Government — 17 U.S.C. § 105)
sources.caption: Representatives of 15 world powers, including German Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann, signing the Kellogg-Briand Pact in Paris renouncing war as an instrument of national policy.
sources.hinge_question: Why did German nationalist parties fiercely denounce Stresemann for signing the Kellogg-Briand Pact when it offered moral protection against foreign invasion?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Nationalist Anti-Young Plan Campaign Poster (Herbert Rothgaengel)
sources.creator: Herbert Rothgaengel / Reichsausschuss für das deutsche Volksbegehren
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Captured 1933–1945 Archival Record / Anonymous Pre-1945 Photograph — NARA RG 242 / USHMM)
sources.caption: Right-wing propaganda poster by Herbert Rothgaengel for the 1929 "Freedom Law" referendum, claiming the Young Plan would enslave German children to pay reparations until 1988.
sources.hinge_question: How did the national campaign against the Young Plan in 1929 allow Adolf Hitler to gain nationwide mainstream political respectability and media coverage?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Confidential Foreign Policy Letter to Crown Prince Wilhelm by Gustav Stresemann
sources.creator: Gustav Stresemann (Foreign Minister of the Weimar Republic)
sources.repository: Political Archive of the Federal Foreign Office (Politisches Archiv des Auswärtigen Amts), Berlin
sources.accession_id: PA AA, Nachlass Gustav Stresemann, Bd. 311
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Historical Diplomatic Correspondence 1925 — CDPA 1988)
sources.caption: Confidential letter written by Weimar Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann to the exiled Crown Prince Wilhelm on 7 September 1925, explaining his diplomatic strategy.
sources.hinge_question: Does Source E prove that Stresemann was a cynical nationalist pretending to be a European peacemaker, or a realistic statesman protecting Germany's vital national interests?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The "New Woman" of the Golden Twenties in Berlin
sources.creator: Ullstein Bild / Berlin Fashion Photographer
sources.repository: Ullstein Bilderdienst / German Federal Archives, Berlin
sources.accession_id: Ullstein Bild No. 00024951 / Berlin Neue Frau c. 1926
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1926 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: The "New Woman" (Neue Frau) in 1920s Berlin: Benefiting from constitutional equality under Article 109, young women embraced financial independence, shorter skirts, and modern clerical employment.
sources.hinge_question: To what extent did the "New Woman" represent a nationwide social revolution, rather than a phenomenon limited to young middle-class women in major cities?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The Bauhaus Architectural Complex in Dessau
sources.creator: Walter Gropius (Architect) / Bauhaus Archive
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1925 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: The Bauhaus at Dessau (1925–1926): Walter Gropius revolutionized architecture by pioneering functional glass-curtain walls, clean steel geometries, and the principle that "form follows function".
sources.hinge_question: Why did modernist institutions like the Bauhaus provoke intense hatred from right-wing traditionalists who viewed internationalist art as "degenerate" (entartet)?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Otto Dix, The Skat Players (Card-Playing War Cripples, 1920)
sources.creator: Otto Dix (1891–1969)
sources.repository: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Neue Nationalgalerie
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1920 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: Otto Dix's famous Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity) painting depicting three severely mutilated Great War veterans playing cards using prosthetic limbs and facial grafts.
sources.hinge_question: How did expressionist artists like Otto Dix challenge both romantic imperial militarism and the superficial consumerism of the Weimar "Golden Twenties"?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Contemporary Analysis of the "New Woman" (Die neue Frau) by Alice Rühle-Gerstel
sources.creator: Alice Rühle-Gerstel (German Psychologist and Social Commentator)
sources.repository: German National Library (Deutsche Nationalbibliothek), Leipzig / Die literarische Welt
sources.accession_id: Die literarische Welt, Berlin, Vol. 3, No. 39 (1927)
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1927 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: Contemporary essay by social commentator Alice Rühle-Gerstel in Die literarische Welt (1927), analysing the real versus superficial emancipation of German women.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the social freedom of the "New Woman" celebrated as a triumph of Weimar democracy by urban liberals, while being fiercely condemned as moral degeneracy by rural conservatives?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Theatrical Release Poster for Fritz Lang's Metropolis (UFA Studios, 1927)
sources.creator: Heinz Schulz-Neudamm / Universum Film AG (UFA)
sources.repository: Deutsche Kinemathek – Museum für Film und Fernsehen, Berlin
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1927 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: Official German release poster for Fritz Lang's dystopian science-fiction film Metropolis, produced by UFA Studios in Babelsberg, illustrating Germany's pioneering cinematic dominance.
sources.hinge_question: How did Fritz Lang's Metropolis reflect Weimar Germany's deep anxiety over industrial modernization, mass mechanization, and class conflict?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The Horseshoe Estate (Hufeisensiedlung) in Berlin-Britz
sources.creator: Bruno Taut & Martin Wagner (Architects)
sources.repository: Landesarchiv Berlin / UNESCO World Heritage Archive
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Published 1925 — Pre-1929 Historical Work)
sources.caption: The Horseshoe Estate in Berlin-Britz, constructed between 1925 and 1930 by socialist architect Bruno Taut to provide affordable, sunlit municipal housing for working-class families.
sources.hinge_question: How did large-scale municipal housing projects like the Hufeisensiedlung demonstrate the social welfare priorities of Weimar local governments?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: German National People's Party (DNVP) Campaign Insignia and Anti-Weimar Symbol (1928)

sources.hinge_question: Why did right-wing traditionalists label modern architecture, jazz, and female independence as "Cultural Bolshevism"?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.1: The Situation on Elizabeth’s Accession, 1558
sources.artifact_title: Queen Elizabeth I Coronation Portrait (1559)
sources.creator: Unknown English Court Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1900 Art)
sources.caption: Queen Elizabeth I in her magnificent gold coronation robes, holding the orb and sceptre as symbols of monarchical authority and divine right, painted c. 1559.
sources.hinge_question: How did Elizabeth use royal portraits like the Coronation Portrait to project divine authority and overcome early doubts about female rule?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.1: The Situation on Elizabeth’s Accession, 1558
sources.artifact_title: Sir William Cecil, Lord Burghley, Elizabeth’s Chief Minister
sources.creator: Marcus Gheeraerts the Elder or Studio
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1900 Art)
sources.caption: Sir William Cecil (1520–1598), created Lord Burghley in 1571, Elizabeth's Secretary of State and closest political confidant for four decades.
sources.hinge_question: What does William Cecil's lifelong appointment as Secretary of State suggest about Elizabeth's reliance on loyal administrative advisors?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.1: The Situation on Elizabeth’s Accession, 1558
sources.artifact_title: Contemporary Portrait of Queen Anne Boleyn (c. 1534)
sources.creator: Unknown English Artist after Holbein
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1900 Art)
sources.caption: Queen Anne Boleyn, mother of Elizabeth I, executed for treason in May 1536, leading Parliament to declare Elizabeth illegitimate.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Catholic contemporaries argue that Henry VIII's marriage to Anne Boleyn rendered Elizabeth illegitimate?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.1: The Situation on Elizabeth’s Accession, 1558
sources.artifact_title: King Henry VIII in Royal Splendour (c. 1540)
sources.creator: Workshop of Hans Holbein the Younger
sources.repository: Walker Art Gallery, National Museums Liverpool
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1900 Art)
sources.caption: King Henry VIII, whose 1544 Third Succession Act reinstated Elizabeth into the line of succession after Edward and Mary, despite remaining legally illegitimate.
sources.hinge_question: How did the 1544 Succession Act passed by Henry VIII restore Elizabeth to the royal line despite her declared illegitimacy?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.1: The Situation on Elizabeth’s Accession, 1558
sources.artifact_title: Queen Mary I and the Inheritance of War and Debt (1554)
sources.creator: Antonis Mor
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1900 Art)
sources.caption: Queen Mary I, whose reign ended in 1558 leaving England £300,000 in debt to Antwerp bankers and bereft of Calais after military disaster against France.
sources.hinge_question: To what extent did the loss of Calais and £300,000 in crown debt under Mary I severely constrain Elizabeth's early foreign policy?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.2: The 'Settlement' of Religion, 1559
sources.artifact_title: The 1559 Act of Supremacy (Parliamentary Roll)
sources.creator: Parliament of England
sources.rights_status: Crown Copyright / Open Parliament Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: The official parchment statute of the 1559 Act of Supremacy passed by Parliament, declaring Elizabeth 'Supreme Governor' of the Church of England.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Elizabeth adopt the title 'Supreme Governor' rather than 'Supreme Head' of the Church of England in the 1559 Act of Supremacy?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.2: The 'Settlement' of Religion, 1559
sources.artifact_title: Title Page of the 1559 Book of Common Prayer
sources.creator: Church of England / Richard Grafton
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Historical Printed Monograph)
sources.caption: Printed title page of the Elizabethan Book of Common Prayer (1559), combining the 1549 and 1552 communion words into a deliberately ambiguous compromise.
sources.hinge_question: How did the ambiguous Communion wording in the 1559 Book of Common Prayer attempt to satisfy both Protestant and Catholic believers?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.2: The 'Settlement' of Religion, 1559
sources.artifact_title: Memorandum by Sir William Cecil on the Uniformity Bill (1559)
sources.creator: Sir William Cecil (State Papers)
sources.rights_status: Open Government Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir William Cecil, who managed the parliamentary strategy to pass the Act of Uniformity through the House of Lords by arresting two Catholic bishops before the vote.
sources.hinge_question: How does Cecil's parliamentary strategy reveal the intense resistance the Elizabethan Settlement faced in the House of Lords?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.2: The 'Settlement' of Religion, 1559
sources.artifact_title: Engraving of the House of Lords Passing the 1559 Settlement
sources.creator: Unknown London Engraver
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Engraving)
sources.caption: Contemporary woodcut engraving of the Elizabethan Parliament assembled in Westminster, debating the Supremacy and Uniformity Bills in the spring of 1559.
sources.hinge_question: How useful is this depiction in illustrating the fragile parliamentary majority that enacted the Act of Uniformity by just three votes?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.2: The 'Settlement' of Religion, 1559
sources.artifact_title: Papal Dispatch of Pope Pius V Condemning the Elizabethan Settlement
sources.creator: El Greco
sources.repository: Vatican Apostolic Archive / Colección Casa de Alba
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Pope Pius V (1504–1572), who viewed the Elizabethan Religious Settlement as an intolerable act of heresy that tore England from Catholic Christendom.
sources.hinge_question: How did the Vatican's refusal to recognise Elizabeth's Church push English Catholics into a crisis of dual loyalty?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.3: Challenge to the Religious Settlement
sources.artifact_title: Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis Excommunicating Elizabeth (1570)
sources.creator: Pope Pius V
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Papal State Document)
sources.caption: The printed Latin text of the Papal Bull Regnans in Excelsis issued by Pope Pius V on 25 February 1570, deposing Elizabeth as a heretic and usurper.
sources.hinge_question: How did Pope Pius V's decree absolving English subjects from allegiance fundamentally transform Catholic worship into treason in the eyes of the Crown?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.3: Challenge to the Religious Settlement
sources.artifact_title: Contemporary Woodcut of Father Edmund Campion SJ at the Tyburn Gallows (1581)
sources.creator: Unknown Catholic Engraver
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Martyrology Woodcut)
sources.caption: Jesuit missionary Father Edmund Campion and his companions being executed for high treason at Tyburn on 1 December 1581.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the Elizabethan government execute Jesuit priests like Edmund Campion as political traitors rather than religious martyrs?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.3: Challenge to the Religious Settlement
sources.artifact_title: Historical Map of Catholic Resistance, Priest Holes, and Seminary Networks

sources.repository: The History Revision Hub Archival Cartography Series
sources.rights_status: Platform Exclusive Archival Asset
sources.caption: Cartographic analysis of Elizabethan England highlighting strongholds of Catholic recusancy in the North and West, and landing points for Douai seminary priests.
sources.hinge_question: What does the geographical distribution of Catholic recusancy indicate about the Crown's struggle to enforce Protestantism in northern England?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.3: Challenge to the Religious Settlement
sources.artifact_title: Portrait of Father Edmund Campion SJ, Catholic Scholar and Priest
sources.creator: Engraver of the Society of Jesus
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Engraved portrait of Father Edmund Campion SJ (1540–1581), whose famous manifesto 'Campion's Brag' insisted his mission was purely spiritual and unconcerned with worldly politics.
sources.hinge_question: What does Campion's open declaration ('Campion's Brag') reveal about the religious zeal driving clandestine Jesuit missions to England?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.3: Challenge to the Religious Settlement
sources.artifact_title: Sir Francis Walsingham’s Surveillance Network on Jesuit Safehouses
sources.creator: John de Critz the Elder
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth's master spy, who recruited double agents and established postal interception networks to track Catholic priests and sympathizers.
sources.hinge_question: How do Walsingham's spy reports corroborate the government's fear that English Catholic manor houses were hubs of rebellion?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.4: The Problem of Mary, Queen of Scots, 1568–69
sources.artifact_title: Portrait of Mary Stuart, Queen of Scots (c. 1565)
sources.creator: Scottish Court Painter
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Mary, Queen of Scots (1542–1587), great-granddaughter of Henry VII, whose arrival in England in May 1568 ignited nineteen years of political crisis for Elizabeth I.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Mary Queen of Scots' arrival in England in May 1568 place Elizabeth in an impossible political and diplomatic dilemma?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.4: The Problem of Mary, Queen of Scots, 1568–69
sources.artifact_title: Sir Francis Walsingham's Intelligence Dossier on Mary Stuart
sources.creator: John de Critz the Elder
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Francis Walsingham, who argued consistently that as long as Mary Stuart lived, Elizabeth's life and the English Protestant church would never be safe.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Protestant hardliners like Walsingham regard Mary's mere physical presence in England as an existential threat to Elizabeth's survival?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.4: The Problem of Mary, Queen of Scots, 1568–69
sources.artifact_title: Portrait of Mary of Guise, Queen Regent of Scotland
sources.creator: French Renaissance School
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Mary of Guise (1515–1560), mother of Mary Queen of Scots, who entrenched French military influence and Catholic power in Scotland during Elizabeth's youth.
sources.hinge_question: How did Mary Stuart's blood ties to the powerful French Guise family amplify English Protestant fears of a Continental invasion?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.4: The Problem of Mary, Queen of Scots, 1568–69
sources.artifact_title: King Francis II of France and Mary's Claim to the English Royal Arms
sources.creator: François Clouet
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: King Francis II of France (1544–1560), first husband of Mary Stuart, who ordered the royal coat of arms of England to be quartered with the arms of France and Scotland.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Mary's quartering of the English royal lions and French fleurs-de-lis on her coat of arms inflame Anglo-French hostilities?

sources.lesson_title: KT 1.4: The Problem of Mary, Queen of Scots, 1568–69
sources.artifact_title: Henri, Duke of Guise, Leader of the French Catholic League
sources.creator: French School / Catholic League
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Henri, 3rd Duke of Guise ('Le Balafré'), Mary Stuart's cousin, who formulated invasion plans with Spain to depose Elizabeth and rescue Mary.
sources.hinge_question: How useful is this source in explaining why English Catholics repeatedly looked to French Catholic dukes to liberate Mary by force?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.1: Plots and Revolts at Home, 1569–1587
sources.artifact_title: Thomas Percy, 7th Earl of Northumberland, Leader of the 1569 Revolt
sources.creator: Unknown English Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Thomas Percy, Earl of Northumberland, who led the 1569 Northern Rebellion, celebrated Catholic Mass in Durham Cathedral, and was executed at York in 1572.
sources.hinge_question: What motivated northern Catholic earls like Northumberland and Westmorland to stage an open rebellion against Elizabeth in November 1569?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.1: Plots and Revolts at Home, 1569–1587
sources.artifact_title: Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk, Executed for the 1571 Ridolfi Plot
sources.creator: Hans Eworth or Follower
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk, England's only duke and premier peer, executed on Tower Hill in June 1572 for his complicity in the Ridolfi Plot.
sources.hinge_question: How did the proposed marriage between the Duke of Norfolk and Mary Queen of Scots connect aristocratic discontent to foreign invasion plots?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.1: Plots and Revolts at Home, 1569–1587
sources.artifact_title: Francis Throckmorton and the 1583 Catholic Conspiracy
sources.creator: Crown Trial Records
sources.rights_status: Open Government Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: Francis Throckmorton, who acted as the key courier between Mary Queen of Scots, the Spanish ambassador Mendoza, and French Catholic invasion planners before his arrest in 1583.
sources.hinge_question: What did Throckmorton's confessions under torture reveal regarding Spanish and French financial backing for an English Catholic insurrection?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.1: Plots and Revolts at Home, 1569–1587
sources.artifact_title: Anthony Babington and the 1586 Conspiracy
sources.creator: Contemporary London Engraver
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Anthony Babington (1561–1586), a young Derbyshire Catholic gentleman who led the conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth and rescue Mary Queen of Scots from Chartley Manor.
sources.hinge_question: How did Babington's plan to assassinate Elizabeth and install Mary Stuart trigger the Bond of Association and lead to Mary's trial?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.1: Plots and Revolts at Home, 1569–1587
sources.artifact_title: Walsingham and Phelippes' Intercepted Babington Cipher Postscript (1586)
sources.creator: Thomas Phelippes
sources.rights_status: Open Government Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: The fatal cipher postscript drawn by code-breaker Thomas Phelippes, adding a gallows mark to Mary Stuart's intercepted letter to Babington asking for the names of the six assassins.
sources.hinge_question: How does cryptographer Thomas Phelippes' deciphered beer-barrel postscript provide decisive forensic evidence of Mary's complicity in regicide?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.2: Relations with Spain, 1569–1585
sources.artifact_title: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, Advocate of Protestant Intervention
sources.creator: Unknown English Court Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester (1532–1588), leader of the interventionist Protestant faction in the Privy Council who commanded English forces in the Netherlands in 1585.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Leicester lobby passionately for English military intervention in the Netherlands while William Cecil urged strategic caution?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.2: Relations with Spain, 1569–1585
sources.artifact_title: Sir Francis Drake, Privateer and Circumnavigator (c. 1581)
sources.creator: Nicholas Hilliard or Follower
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Francis Drake (1540–1596), privateer and explorer knighted by Elizabeth in 1581 after capturing hundreds of thousands of pounds in Spanish bullion.
sources.hinge_question: How did Elizabeth's public knighting of Drake aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford signal open defiance against Spanish imperial claims?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.2: Relations with Spain, 1569–1585
sources.artifact_title: Sir John Hawkins, Naval Commander and Atlantic Privateer
sources.creator: Unknown English Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir John Hawkins (1532–1595), who pioneered transatlantic slave voyages and served as Treasurer of the Navy, revolutionizing English galleon design.
sources.hinge_question: How did the 1568 Spanish attack on Hawkins and Drake at San Juan de Ulúa set off decades of undeclared maritime warfare?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.2: Relations with Spain, 1569–1585
sources.artifact_title: Jodocus Hondius's 1595 Map of Drake’s Global Circumnavigation and Raids
sources.creator: Jodocus Hondius
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Engraved world map by Jodocus Hondius celebrating Francis Drake's 1577–1580 circumnavigation, raiding Spanish ports in Chile, Peru, and California.
sources.hinge_question: How does this commemorative chart demonstrate the psychological impact of English privateers penetrating the 'Spanish Lake' of the Pacific?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.2: Relations with Spain, 1569–1585
sources.artifact_title: Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma, Commander of the Army of Flanders
sources.creator: Otto van Veen
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Alexander Farnese, Prince and Duke of Parma (1545–1592), whose brilliant recapture of Antwerp in 1585 forced Elizabeth to intervene militarily via the Treaty of Nonsuch.
sources.hinge_question: How did Parma's brutal reconquest of Dutch cities like Antwerp compel Elizabeth to sign the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.3: The Outbreak of War with Spain, 1585–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir Francis Drake Planning the Pre-emptive Raid on Cadiz (1587)
sources.creator: Unknown Maritime Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Francis Drake, appointed Vice-Admiral by Elizabeth with royal orders to disrupt Spanish naval preparations for the invasion of England in 1587.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Drake describe his destruction of Spanish supplies at Cadiz as 'singeing the King of Spain's beard'?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.3: The Outbreak of War with Spain, 1585–1588
sources.artifact_title: Queen Elizabeth I Addressing the Troops at Tilbury (August 1588)
sources.creator: Eyewitness account / Engraving
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Queen Elizabeth I on horseback reviewing 17,000 militia troops assembled at West Tilbury in August 1588 to resist a Spanish landing.
sources.hinge_question: How did Elizabeth's Tilbury speech turn her gender from a perceived weakness into a rallying cry for national unity?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.3: The Outbreak of War with Spain, 1585–1588
sources.artifact_title: Alonso Pérez de Guzmán, 7th Duke of Medina Sidonia
sources.creator: Spanish Court Painter
sources.repository: Palacio Ducal de Medina Sidonia, Sanlúcar
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: The Duke of Medina Sidonia, appointed supreme commander of the Spanish Armada by King Philip II following the sudden death of the Marquis of Santa Cruz in February 1588.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Medina Sidonia write to King Philip II expressing severe doubts about his own ability to command the Grand Armada?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.3: The Outbreak of War with Spain, 1585–1588
sources.artifact_title: Robert Dudley Organizing the Militia Camp at West Tilbury (1588)
sources.creator: English Workshop Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, appointed Lieutenant-General of the Queen's Armies, who oversaw the fortification and troop deployment at Tilbury Fort in 1588.
sources.hinge_question: What does Dudley's correspondence reveal about the logistical chaos and food shortages plaguing English defensive troops in Essex?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.3: The Outbreak of War with Spain, 1585–1588
sources.artifact_title: Parma’s Army of Flanders Assembled on the Coast of Dunkirk (1588)
sources.creator: Dutch School Engraver
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: The Duke of Parma, whose 27,000 veteran infantry were assembled in flat-bottomed barges at Dunkirk and Nieuwpoort waiting for the Armada to clear the English fleet.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the Armada completely dependent on rendezvous with Parma's barges at Dunkirk to mount an invasion of England?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.4: The Spanish Armada: Strategy, Conflict & Defeat, 1588
sources.artifact_title: The Battle of Gravelines and the Fireships (8 August 1588)
sources.creator: English School Maritime Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: The decisive Battle of Gravelines: English race-built warships engaging the scattered Spanish galleons at close range after fireships disrupted their defensive formation.
sources.hinge_question: How did the English fireship attack off Calais effectively shatter the Armada's defensive crescent formation?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.4: The Spanish Armada: Strategy, Conflict & Defeat, 1588
sources.artifact_title: The Armada Portrait of Queen Elizabeth I (1588)
sources.creator: George Gower, Serjeant Painter
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I, painted by George Gower c. 1588, with her hand resting upon the globe and the defeat of the Armada depicted in the background windows.
sources.hinge_question: How do the visual symbols in the Armada Portrait (hand resting on the globe, sunlit calmness vs stormy shipwreck) celebrate English naval triumph?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.4: The Spanish Armada: Strategy, Conflict & Defeat, 1588
sources.artifact_title: Cartographic Routes and Shipwrecks of the Spanish Armada (1588)

sources.hinge_question: Why did severe Atlantic gales and uncharted rocky coastlines inflict catastrophic losses on the retreating Spanish fleet off Ireland?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.4: The Spanish Armada: Strategy, Conflict & Defeat, 1588
sources.artifact_title: Duke of Medina Sidonia's Post-Action Report to King Philip II (1588)
sources.creator: Spanish Court Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Portrait of Medina Sidonia, whose confidential report to King Philip II in September 1588 lamented that only 67 out of 130 ships and fewer than 10,000 men returned to Spain.
sources.hinge_question: To what extent did lack of deep-water ports and communication breakdowns with Parma undermine Medina Sidonia's campaign?

sources.lesson_title: KT 2.4: The Spanish Armada: Strategy, Conflict & Defeat, 1588
sources.artifact_title: Queen Elizabeth in Triumphal Procession to St Paul's Cathedral (1588)
sources.creator: London Printmaker
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Queen Elizabeth I riding in an open chariot to St Paul's Cathedral in November 1588 to give public thanks for the deliverance of England from the Spanish Armada.
sources.hinge_question: How did the English Crown exploit the motto 'He blew with his winds and they were scattered' to prove God favoured Protestant England?

sources.caption: Queen Elizabeth carried in an open litter by six knights and surrounded by Garter Knights and courtiers in lavish Renaissance attire, painted c. 1601.

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.1: Education and Leisure in Elizabethan England, 1558–1588

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.1: Education and Leisure in Elizabethan England, 1558–1588

sources.caption: Woodcut illustration of an Elizabethan polygonal outdoor playhouse with the flag hoisted to indicate an afternoon theatrical performance.
sources.hinge_question: Why were Elizabethan commercial theatres deliberately built outside the City of London's jurisdiction in Southwark?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.1: Education and Leisure in Elizabethan England, 1558–1588

sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Thomas Harriot (1560–1621), Oxford-educated mathematician, navigation tutor to Sir Walter Raleigh, and pioneer of English empirical science.
sources.hinge_question: How did the expansion of grammar schools and Oxford colleges contribute to the rise of English scientific inquiry in the Elizabethan era?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.1: Education and Leisure in Elizabethan England, 1558–1588

sources.caption: Printed botanical engravings from an Elizabethan herbarium, illustrating the study of medicinal plants, gardening, and empirical natural philosophy.
sources.hinge_question: How does the publication of vernacular botanical and herbal treatises demonstrate the broadening intellectual curiosity of Elizabethan gentry?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588

sources.rights_status: Public Domain

sources.hinge_question: Why did Thomas Harman publish detailed classifications of rogues and vagabonds like 'Abraham Men' and 'Counterfeit Cranks'?

sources.hinge_question: How did the 1601 Poor Law create a formal national system that distinguished between the 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588

sources.caption: Sixteenth-century woodcut illustrating the public punishment of vagrants: tied to the end of a cart and stripped to the waist to be flogged.

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: William Cecil's Parliamentary Memoranda on Grain Inflation and Enclosure (1570s)
sources.creator: Sir William Cecil (State Papers)
sources.rights_status: Open Government Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir William Cecil, who recognized that population growth, debasement of coinage, and sheep enclosure caused devastating grain price inflation and rural unemployment.
sources.hinge_question: How do Cecil's private notes show that ministers recognized economic factors like poor harvests and enclosure drove rural poverty?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Quarter Sessions Records of Justices of the Peace in Norfolk
sources.creator: Clerk of the Peace, Norfolk
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Norfolk county magistrate records documenting the appointment of searchers to apprehend masterless men and supervise parish work schemes.
sources.hinge_question: How do local magistrates' court records corroborate the claim that vagrancy laws were enforced unevenly across different English counties?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: English Naval Galleons with Low-Profile Race-Built Hulls (c. 1585)
sources.creator: Naval Architectural Draftsman
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Naval engraving showing the design of John Hawkins' innovative race-built galleons: lower forecastles, streamlined keels, and heavier broadside guns.
sources.hinge_question: How did John Hawkins' race-built galleons give English navigators decisive technical advantages in speed and weatherly sailing?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir Francis Drake with Navigational Compass and Terrestrial Globe
sources.creator: Jodocus Hondius
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Portrait of Sir Francis Drake holding a mariner's compass beside an open terrestrial globe, painted by Jodocus Hondius c. 1583.
sources.hinge_question: How does Drake's deliberate inclusion of the compass and globe promote England's ambition to rival the Spanish Empire globally?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Augustine Ryther's Sea Chart of the English Channel and Atlantic Approaches
sources.creator: Augustine Ryther
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Engraved maritime chart by Augustine Ryther (1590) displaying coastal soundings, compass roses, and latitude lines along the Atlantic seaboard.
sources.hinge_question: What does this navigational chart indicate about the growing cartographic accuracy available to late Elizabethan ship captains?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir John Hawkins, Treasurer of the Royal Navy and Slave Trade Pioneer
sources.creator: West Country Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir John Hawkins, who led three transatlantic slave-trading voyages between 1562 and 1568, backed secretly by Queen Elizabeth and London syndicates.
sources.hinge_question: How did Hawkins' early triangular slave trade voyages in the 1560s establish the commercial and naval foundations of English oceanic expansion?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir Richard Grenville, Vice-Admiral and Commander of the 1585 Virginia Expedition
sources.creator: Unknown English Artist
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Richard Grenville (1542–1591), fierce naval commander who transported the first English colonists to Roanoke Island in 1585 in the Tiger.
sources.hinge_question: How does Grenville's dual career as a naval combatant and colonial commander reflect the militarized nature of Elizabethan maritime expansion?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: Sir Walter Raleigh, Courtier, Explorer, and Coloniser (c. 1588)
sources.creator: Nicholas Hilliard or Workshop
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Walter Raleigh (1554–1618), royal favourite who received a royal patent from Elizabeth in 1584 granting him exclusive rights to colonize 'Virginia'.
sources.hinge_question: Why was Sir Walter Raleigh unable to lead the Virginia colonization expeditions in person despite holding the royal patent from Elizabeth?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: The Roanoke Island Colony Map by John White (1585)
sources.creator: John White
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: John White's detailed watercolor map of the coast of Virginia and North Carolina from Cape Lookout to the Chesapeake Bay, surveyed in 1585.
sources.hinge_question: How does John White's detailed chart of the Outer Banks explain why treacherous shoals caused the flagship Tiger to run aground and ruin food supplies?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: John White Watercolor of an Algonquin Chief (Herowan / Werowance) of Roanoke (1585)
sources.creator: John White
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: John White's watercolor of a coastal Algonquin chief (herowan) adorned with copper ornaments, feathers, and body paint, painted from life in 1585.
sources.hinge_question: What does White's portrait of an indigenous leader reveal about initial English intentions to study and engage with local tribes?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: John White's Painting of an Algonquin Religious Feast and Dance at Secotan
sources.creator: John White
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Watercolor by John White depicting a ritual circle dance of Algonquin priests and dancers with carved posts surrounding the sacred ceremonial ground at Secotan.
sources.hinge_question: How reliable is John White's artwork as primary ethnographical evidence of pre-colonial Native American culture?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: John White Watercolor of an Algonquin Man and Woman Eating at Meat (1585)
sources.creator: John White
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Watercolor by John White showing an Algonquin couple seated on a reed mat eating a meal of boiled maize, fish, and tobacco.
sources.hinge_question: How does White's depiction of indigenous maize and dietary habits corroborate Thomas Harriot's written report on the agricultural potential of Virginia?
